Thanks again for the quick call today — great overview. A couple of clarifications from our SRE team:

- Target: 95th percentile request latency for streaming chat responses should be <= 200ms.
- Concurrency: we expect ~150 steady concurrent users (typing/streaming) with peaks up to ~2,000 concurrent connections for 3-5 minutes during launches.
- Throughput: typical average QPS is ~120, but peaks may hit ~2k for short bursts.
- Warm pools: we can't tolerate long cold starts; anything over ~30s for capacity scale-up will be disruptive.

Can you confirm whether Redwood supports a warm pool / pre-warmed workers model, typical scale-up times from zero, and queueing behavior when capacity is constrained? Also attaching our SLO spreadsheet.

Samir — thanks for the clear SLOs and the spreadsheet, that helps a lot. Quick recap from our side and concrete answers now, followed by next steps: 

Recap (what we heard)
- P95 streaming latency target: <= 200ms
- Steady concurrency: ~150 users; burst concurrency up to ~2,000 for 3-5 minutes
- Average throughput: ~120 QPS (baseline); peak bursts up to ~2k QPS
- Requirement: minimal cold-start impact (prefer <30s scale-up) and predictable queueing behavior during scale events

Short answers: 
- Warm pools: yes — Redwood Dedicated supports configurable warm pools (pre-provisioned workers) that keep GPU VMs and runtime processes hot to minimize cold-starts. You can size warm pools by instance/pod counts or by token throughput.
- Scale-up times: from idle with warm pool size 0 -> cold spin-up is typically 90–180s (VM + runtime warm). With a small warm pool (1–3 warm workers), observed scale-to-higher-capacity times are ~15–45s to add more workers and accept traffic; fullness depends on cloud provider VM startup and image caching.
- Queueing behavior: when capacity is saturated we apply short in-memory request queueing with per-customer prioritization and tail-drop policies. We surface queue length and estimated wait-time via metrics; we also support soft-throttles (429s) with retry-backoff guidance and automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants if configured.

Attachments: I attached a short note with recommended warm-pool sizes based on your concurrency/throughput numbers. Dev (cc) will sketch an initial config for your PoC.

Next steps: 
1) Dev to propose an initial Dedicated config (warm pool, instance types, autoscale policy) => by EOD tomorrow.
2) We run a short load test (we'll provide a runner) against your PoC integration to validate P95 latency at target concurrency.
3) If that looks good, procurement can review pricing for a 2-month reserved capacity PoC.

Does that timeline work? If there are any constraints on allowed instance families or VPC settings, send them over.

Thanks,
Marissa

Samir / Marissa — following up with the initial recommended config for PoC warm pools and autoscaling. TL;DR: small warm pool + aggressive scale policy to meet your 30s requirement while controlling cost.

Recommended starting config (PoC):
- Baseline capacity: 4 warm workers (NVIDIA A10 equivalent) to handle ~200 steady concurrent streaming sessions with low tail latency.
- Burst capacity: autoscale to add up to 40 workers in response to queue depth and CPU/GPU utilization; scale actions are executed in parallel to reduce serial startup penalty.
- Scale policy: reactive scale on CPU/GPU utilization and queue depth with burst policy that allows adding workers 4 at a time and up to 8 in parallel (empirically reduces scale time to ~20–35s once warm pool is non-zero).
- Cold start: if warm pool = 0, cold spin-up (new VMs + runtime) ~90–150s depending on cloud image cache.
- Queueing: per-tenant FIFO queue with soft priority for streaming (short timeouts, 10–15s) and immediate 429 after max wait; metrics exported: queue_length, queue_latency_p95, worker_start_time, worker_ready_time.

Notes: these numbers assume model variants that fit on A10-class GPUs with optimized kernels; high-memory models or multi-gpu shards will increase start-up and scale times. For the PoC we recommend using a quantized variant we have validated for low-latency streaming.

I'll prepare an infra-as-code snippet and a small load test script (k6-based) that reproduces burst patterns — will send in the next message.

—Dev

Lisa / Samir — great questions, quick answers and action items below.

Billing for warm pools: Yes — warm workers are billed at the same instance rate while they are reserved/hot. For PoC we can offer an credit-backed discount on the warm pool hours (I will propose % credit in the procurement doc). We also provide tooling to automatically scale down warm pools during known off-hours to control cost.

VPC placement: Absolutely — Dedicated and Private deployments support customer VPC placement. Warm workers can be provisioned into your subnet with customer-controlled security groups and egress rules. We'll need a short list of allowed CIDRs and any required NAT/egress gateways.

Load test harness: Dev will push the k6 script + runner and a small Docker image you can run inside your environment that generates the 3–5 minute 2k-concurrency burst. We'll include knobs for ramp-up, payload size, and streaming concurrency (per-connection chunking).

Action items:

- Dev: upload k6 script + infra-as-code snippet to the HubSpot deal and a short runbook (tomorrow).
- Acme: share subnet/CIDR and any egress constraints (EOD tomorrow).

I'll also attach the SLO spreadsheet we discussed (attached). If everyone is aligned I'll schedule a 30-min sync tomorrow to kick off the PoC.

Thanks all — looking forward to running this.
